deduped_items.title: Les héros controversés de la Seconde Guerre mondiale au Japon : un pilote kamikaze témoigne
deduped_items.summary: Alors que la Seconde Guerre mondiale touche à sa fin, les troupes américaines avancent et les forces japonaises s’épuisent. Des milliers de pilotes japonais, âgés en moyenne de 21 ans, reçoivent alors l’ordre de lancer leur avion chargé d’explosifs sur les navires de guerre ennemis. Plus de 3 800 pilotes ont sacrifié leur vie, 7 000 marins alliés ont été tués. Notre reporter Mélodie Sforza est allée à la rencontre de l’un des derniers pilotes kamikazes encore en vie.

deduped_items.title: Vince Gilligan, auteur de « Breaking Bad » : « J’adore que les téléspectateurs et les critiques expliquent mes propres séries »
deduped_items.summary: « Artistes à l’œuvre » (6/6). Le showrunneur américain, créateur de plusieurs séries télévisées à succès comme « Breaking Bad », « Better Call Saul » et, plus récemment, « Pluribus », aime forger des histoires et des personnages uniques, à contre-courant. Après plus de trente ans passés dans l’industrie du divertissement, il caresse l’espoir que son travail lui survive, explique-t-il, dans un entretien au « Monde ».

Lille reçoit le Paris Saint-Germain ce vendredi en ouverture de la deuxième journée de Ligue 1. Le Losc voudra enchaîner après sa très belle victoire face à Angers (2-0) la semaine dernière tandis que Paris aura à cœur de se reprendre après le match nul concédé à Rennes (2-2) et enfin lancer sa saison. 20’
Le nouveau numéro 9 du PSG est dans tous les bons coups sur ce début de match. Hakimi le trouve dans la surface, l'Espagnol reprend en première intention mais ça fuit le cadre.
18’
Il est aussi difficile à suivre que son frère sur ce début de match ! Encore une fois, Ethan Mbappé s'échappe dans la profondeur, la défense du PSG se fait aspirer. Le dernier geste manque de puissance pour inquiéter Safonov.
15’
On a pris l'habitude de voir les Parisiens dominer la possession du ballon, c'est bien le cas sur ce premier quart d'heure de jeu.
12’
Une statistique pour illuster la fragilité du LOSC à Pierre Mauroy ces derniers mois. En 2026, les Dogues n'ont pris que 10 points à domicile. Le 14e bilan de Ligue 1 sur la période l'an dernier.
9’
On assiste à un début de match très rythmé, avec des Lillois qui n'hésitent pas à presser assez haut. Cela a failli coûter cher... mais aussi faire craquer le PSG quelques minutes plus tard. Toujours 0-0 !
7’
Les Lillois répliquent immédiatement, Ethan Mbappé se joue de Marquinhos et centre vers Giroud, qui reprend en première intention ! L'attaquant du LOSC bute sur Safonov, qui a pris beaucoup d'espace en sortant de sa cage ! Quel arrêt du Russe !
5’
Ferran Torres prend la profondeur et devance Alexsandro, Ozer sort dans les pieds de l'Espagnol mais relâche le ballon. Hakimi s'en empare et frappe, ça vient mourir sur le poteau extérieur droit !! Grosse chaleur pour le LOSC !
4’
Le portier russe s'est fait peur à l'échauffement en heurtant lourdement l'entraîneur des gardiens du PSG, Borja Alvarez. Il tient bien sa place, avec un strap apparent au niveau des cervicales.
2’
Les indications tactiques à l'échauffement étaient les bonnes : Zaïre-Emery va semble t-il bien évoluer dans le couloir gauche alors que Beraldo prend place au milieu.
1’
Le coup d'envoi de ce choc Lille-PSG, match d'ouverture de la J2, est donné ! Avec 15 minutes de retard on le rappelle, cela fait suite à un problème technique de la billetterie lilloise. Ce sont les Dogues qui engagent.
20h50
20h43
Assez incroyable ce qui passe devant Pierre-Mauroy. Des dizaines de supporters lillois sont bloqués, ne peuvent vraisemblablement pas accéder à leurs billets et doivent donc passer par la billetterie du stade.
20h34
Le coup d'envoi, initialement prévu à 20h45, est retardé de 15 minutes. Cela fait suite à des problèmes de billetterie à Lille.
20h33
C'est la première de son fils Davide à domicile.
20h25
À l’échauffement Zaire-Emery est latéral gauche, Beraldo en sentinelle et Akliouche sur le côté droit de l’attaque.
AP
Le PSG affiche une certaine fragilité défensive ces dernières semaines : le club parisien a encaissé au moins un but lors de ses 7 derniers matchs. Une série qui illustre une défense devenue particulièrement friable, capable de laisser des espaces à ses adversaires.
20h22
Espérons pour le gardien russe que ce ne soit pas trop grave
20h17
Non seulement en attaque bien sûr, ou il n'aligne ni Barcola, ni Kvara, ni Mika Godts à gauche, mais aussi en défense, toujours à gauche, où, après avoir titularisé Lucas Hernandez au premier match, il met Lucas Beraldo, laissant encore Lucas Digne sur le banc.
20h12
Le gardien a laissé un excellent souvenir à Lille.
Lille n’a plus battu Paris depuis sa victoire 1-0 en avril 2021. À domicile, la disette est encore plus longue, puisque les Dogues n’ont plus vaincu le PSG depuis le mémorable 5-1 d’avril 2019

On a pris l'habitude de voir les Parisiens dominer la possession du ballon, c'est bien le cas sur ce premier quart d'heure de jeu.

Une statistique pour illuster la fragilité du LOSC à Pierre Mauroy ces derniers mois. En 2026, les Dogues n'ont pris que 10 points à domicile. Le 14e bilan de Ligue 1 sur la période l'an dernier.
9’
On assiste à un début de match très rythmé, avec des Lillois qui n'hésitent pas à presser assez haut. Cela a failli coûter cher... mais aussi faire craquer le PSG quelques minutes plus tard. Toujours 0-0 !
7’
Les Lillois répliquent immédiatement, Ethan Mbappé se joue de Marquinhos et centre vers Giroud, qui reprend en première intention ! L'attaquant du LOSC bute sur Safonov, qui a pris beaucoup d'espace en sortant de sa cage ! Quel arrêt du Russe !

Ferran Torres prend la profondeur et devance Alexsandro, Ozer sort dans les pieds de l'Espagnol mais relâche le ballon. Hakimi s'en empare et frappe, ça vient mourir sur le poteau extérieur droit !! Grosse chaleur pour le LOSC !

2’

20h34

20h33

20h25
À l’échauffement Zaire-Emery est latéral gauche, Beraldo en sentinelle et Akliouche sur le côté droit de l’attaque.
AP

20h12

Le nouveau numéro 9 du PSG est dans tous les bons coups sur ce début de match. Hakimi le trouve dans la surface, l'Espagnol reprend en première intention mais ça fuit le cadre.
18’
Il est aussi difficile à suivre que son frère sur ce début de match ! Encore une fois, Ethan Mbappé s'échappe dans la profondeur, la défense du PSG se fait aspirer. Le dernier geste manque de puissance pour inquiéter Safonov.
15’
On a pris l'habitude de voir les Parisiens dominer la possession du ballon, c'est bien le cas sur ce premier quart d'heure de jeu.
12’
Une statistique pour illuster la fragilité du LOSC à Pierre Mauroy ces derniers mois. En 2026, les Dogues n'ont pris que 10 points à domicile. Le 14e bilan de Ligue 1 sur la période l'an dernier.
9’
On assiste à un début de match très rythmé, avec des Lillois qui n'hésitent pas à presser assez haut. Cela a failli coûter cher... mais aussi faire craquer le PSG quelques minutes plus tard. Toujours 0-0 !
7’
Les Lillois répliquent immédiatement, Ethan Mbappé se joue de Marquinhos et centre vers Giroud, qui reprend en première intention ! L'attaquant du LOSC bute sur Safonov, qui a pris beaucoup d'espace en sortant de sa cage ! Quel arrêt du Russe !
5’
Ferran Torres prend la profondeur et devance Alexsandro, Ozer sort dans les pieds de l'Espagnol mais relâche le ballon. Hakimi s'en empare et frappe, ça vient mourir sur le poteau extérieur droit !! Grosse chaleur pour le LOSC !
4’
Le portier russe s'est fait peur à l'échauffement en heurtant lourdement l'entraîneur des gardiens du PSG, Borja Alvarez. Il tient bien sa place, avec un strap apparent au niveau des cervicales.
2’
Les indications tactiques à l'échauffement étaient les bonnes : Zaïre-Emery va semble t-il bien évoluer dans le couloir gauche alors que Beraldo prend place au milieu.
1’
Le coup d'envoi de ce choc Lille-PSG, match d'ouverture de la J2, est donné ! Avec 15 minutes de retard on le rappelle, cela fait suite à un problème technique de la billetterie lilloise. Ce sont les Dogues qui engagent.
20h50
20h43
Assez incroyable ce qui passe devant Pierre-Mauroy. Des dizaines de supporters lillois sont bloqués, ne peuvent vraisemblablement pas accéder à leurs billets et doivent donc passer par la billetterie du stade.
20h34
Le coup d'envoi, initialement prévu à 20h45, est retardé de 15 minutes. Cela fait suite à des problèmes de billetterie à Lille.
20h33
C'est la première de son fils Davide à domicile.
20h25
À l’échauffement Zaire-Emery est latéral gauche, Beraldo en sentinelle et Akliouche sur le côté droit de l’attaque.
AP
Le PSG affiche une certaine fragilité défensive ces dernières semaines : le club parisien a encaissé au moins un but lors de ses 7 derniers matchs. Une série qui illustre une défense devenue particulièrement friable, capable de laisser des espaces à ses adversaires.
20h22
Espérons pour le gardien russe que ce ne soit pas trop grave
20h17
Non seulement en attaque bien sûr, ou il n'aligne ni Barcola, ni Kvara, ni Mika Godts à gauche, mais aussi en défense, toujours à gauche, où, après avoir titularisé Lucas Hernandez au premier match, il met Lucas Beraldo, laissant encore Lucas Digne sur le banc.
20h12
Le gardien a laissé un excellent souvenir à Lille.
Lille n’a plus battu Paris depuis sa victoire 1-0 en avril 2021. À domicile, la disette est encore plus longue, puisque les Dogues n’ont plus vaincu le PSG depuis le mémorable 5-1 d’avril 2019

Le nouveau numéro 9 du PSG est dans tous les bons coups sur ce début de match. Hakimi le trouve dans la surface, l'Espagnol reprend en première intention mais ça fuit le cadre.
18’
Il est aussi difficile à suivre que son frère sur ce début de match ! Encore une fois, Ethan Mbappé s'échappe dans la profondeur, la défense du PSG se fait aspirer. Le dernier geste manque de puissance pour inquiéter Safonov.
15’
On a pris l'habitude de voir les Parisiens dominer la possession du ballon, c'est bien le cas sur ce premier quart d'heure de jeu.
12’
Une statistique pour illuster la fragilité du LOSC à Pierre Mauroy ces derniers mois. En 2026, les Dogues n'ont pris que 10 points à domicile. Le 14e bilan de Ligue 1 sur la période l'an dernier.
9’
On assiste à un début de match très rythmé, avec des Lillois qui n'hésitent pas à presser assez haut. Cela a failli coûter cher... mais aussi faire craquer le PSG quelques minutes plus tard. Toujours 0-0 !
7’
Les Lillois répliquent immédiatement, Ethan Mbappé se joue de Marquinhos et centre vers Giroud, qui reprend en première intention ! L'attaquant du LOSC bute sur Safonov, qui a pris beaucoup d'espace en sortant de sa cage ! Quel arrêt du Russe !
5’
Ferran Torres prend la profondeur et devance Alexsandro, Ozer sort dans les pieds de l'Espagnol mais relâche le ballon. Hakimi s'en empare et frappe, ça vient mourir sur le poteau extérieur droit !! Grosse chaleur pour le LOSC !
4’
Le portier russe s'est fait peur à l'échauffement en heurtant lourdement l'entraîneur des gardiens du PSG, Borja Alvarez. Il tient bien sa place, avec un strap apparent au niveau des cervicales.
2’
Les indications tactiques à l'échauffement étaient les bonnes : Zaïre-Emery va semble t-il bien évoluer dans le couloir gauche alors que Beraldo prend place au milieu.
1’
Le coup d'envoi de ce choc Lille-PSG, match d'ouverture de la J2, est donné ! Avec 15 minutes de retard on le rappelle, cela fait suite à un problème technique de la billetterie lilloise. Ce sont les Dogues qui engagent.
20h50
20h43
Assez incroyable ce qui passe devant Pierre-Mauroy. Des dizaines de supporters lillois sont bloqués, ne peuvent vraisemblablement pas accéder à leurs billets et doivent donc passer par la billetterie du stade.
20h34
Le coup d'envoi, initialement prévu à 20h45, est retardé de 15 minutes. Cela fait suite à des problèmes de billetterie à Lille.
20h33
C'est la première de son fils Davide à domicile.
20h25
À l’échauffement Zaire-Emery est latéral gauche, Beraldo en sentinelle et Akliouche sur le côté droit de l’attaque.
AP
Le PSG affiche une certaine fragilité défensive ces dernières semaines : le club parisien a encaissé au moins un but lors de ses 7 derniers matchs. Une série qui illustre une défense devenue particulièrement friable, capable de laisser des espaces à ses adversaires.
20h22
Espérons pour le gardien russe que ce ne soit pas trop grave
20h17
Non seulement en attaque bien sûr, ou il n'aligne ni Barcola, ni Kvara, ni Mika Godts à gauche, mais aussi en défense, toujours à gauche, où, après avoir titularisé Lucas Hernandez au premier match, il met Lucas Beraldo, laissant encore Lucas Digne sur le banc.
20h12
Le gardien a laissé un excellent souvenir à Lille.
Lille n’a plus battu Paris depuis sa victoire 1-0 en avril 2021. À domicile, la disette est encore plus longue, puisque les Dogues n’ont plus vaincu le PSG depuis le mémorable 5-1 d’avril 2019

deduped_items.body_text:
WASHINGTON: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Friday warned that any attempt to deprive Pakistan of waters “rightfully allocated to it” under the Indus Waters Treaty would have “profound consequences for regional peace and security”.
The IWT has come under strain since India announced in 2025 that it was placing its treaty obligations in abeyance. The announcement followed an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 tourists — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence. For its part, Pakistan strongly denied the allegations and called for a neutral investigation.
In his virtual address to a Washington seminar on “The Indus Waters Treaty: South Asian Security at the Crossroads”, he declared that Pakistan would strongly safeguard its “legitimate rights and interests” under the treaty and international law.
FM Dar said the 1960 agreement remained “valid, binding and fully operative” despite India’s unilateral decision in April 2025 to place it “in abeyance”.
“The treaty contains no provision permitting either party to unilaterally suspend or place it in abeyance,” he said, adding that neither country could, “through a unilateral political declaration, extinguish obligations solemnly undertaken under international law.”
FM Dar said the issue went beyond the bilateral relationship, arguing that it concerned “the sanctity of treaties” and “confidence in international law”.
“If solemn treaty obligations can simply be set aside whenever political relations deteriorate, the very purpose of concluding the treaties is undermined,” he said.
He also stressed that geography made cooperation unavoidable, noting that “states cannot alter the direction in which rivers flow”.
“That is precisely why rules matter,” FM Dar said, urging the international community to preserve treaty-based water governance in South Asia.
The foreign minister further said the treaty had survived wars, military crises, diplomatic breakdowns and prolonged political tensions for more than six decades because both countries had understood that water on which “hundreds of millions of lives depend” was too fundamental to be subjected to fluctuations in political relations.
“Today, however, that principle faces its gravest challenge,” he said.
FM Dar said Pakistan’s position was clear and consistent and that treaty-based proceedings had continued despite India’s assertion of “abeyance”, reinforcing the principle that “unilateral action cannot displace an agreed legal framework”.
Pakistan has pursued arbitration over disputes concerning Indian hydroelectric projects on the Western Rivers, particularly Kishenganga and Ratle.
The Court of Arbitration at The Hague has continued proceedings, with earlier rulings addressing its jurisdiction and questions concerning the interpretation and application of the treaty.
The treaty allocates the three eastern rivers to India and the three western rivers, including the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, primarily to Pakistan, subject to specified Indian uses.
FM Dar said resorting to the Permanent Indus Commission, a neutral expert or a Court of Arbitration “is not an act of confrontation” but “the implementation of the very legal framework to which both countries agreed and are bound”.
“Pakistan has consistently sought to resolve differences through dialogue, diplomacy and the mechanisms provided under the Treaty,” he said.
He said the dispute was especially serious because Pakistan’s agriculture, food security, energy production, livelihoods and economic development depended heavily on the Indus River system.
“The Indus Basin is the lifeline of more than 250 million Pakistanis,” Dar said. “Water security for Pakistan is therefore inseparable from economic security, food security and, ultimately, national security.”

deduped_items.title: Michael Jordan's 1998 NBA Finals sneakers sell for a record $2.2 million
deduped_items.summary: In 1998, Michael Jordan laced up a pair of his iconic black and red Air Jordan 13s to bring home a Bulls victory during Game 2 of his final NBA championship — and now they are the most expensive sneakers ever to sell at auction. The game-winning sneakers sold for $2.2 million at Sotheby's in New York on Tuesday, smashing the sneaker auction record of $1.47 million, set in 2021 by a pair of Nike Air Ships that Jordan wore earlier in his career.

deduped_items.title: EXCLUSIVE: ‘Delete From The Deleted File’ — Fauci Tried To Destroy Gain-Of-Function Research Email, New Docs Reveal
deduped_items.summary: EXCLUSIVE: ‘Delete From The Deleted File’ — Fauci Tried To Destroy Gain-Of-Function Research Email, New Docs Reveal
deduped_items.body_text:
Eight years before COVID emerged, a journalist issued a prophetic warning that risky viral research could usher in “doomsday” and damage the reputation of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Anthony Fauci groused in an email to an aide about that warning, then instructed the aide to permanently delete the exchange, documents obtained by the Daily Caller News Foundation show.
The documents add to growing evidence that Fauci destroyed public records despite his sworn testimony that he never did. Deleting government records violates federal law.
Fauci did not respond to a request for comment.
In 2011, the advent of gain-of-function research — experiments that make viruses more infectious or deadly in the lab — caused its first major controversy. With funding from Fauci’s institute at the NIH, Dutch virologist Ron Fouchier had made an airborne strain of a bird flu with an estimated 50% fatality rate, which he described as “probably one of the most dangerous viruses you can make.”
Fauci and New York Times science writer Phil Boffey traded barbs in newspaper opinion pages about the work. (RELATED: Fauci’s Warm Relationship With Intel Community Exposed In Declassified Docs)
Manmade pandemic viruses are a “risk worth taking,” Fauci insisted in a December 2011 Washington Post editorial, because they could help drugmakers and public health get a jump start if they emerge in nature. NIH Director Francis Collins and National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Vaccine Research Center Gary Nabel co-authored the op-ed.
The New York Times published an op-ed apparently written by Boffey in January 2012 arguing that NIH created an “engineered doomsday” that could kill “hundreds of millions of people.” The new emails reveal the author of the un-bylined op-ed for the first time.
“The consequences, should the virus escape, are too devastating to risk,” he said in an apparent reference to the title of Fauci’s op-ed.
Boffey wrote a follow-up in March 2012 titled “The Truth About the Doomsday Virus?” Under scrutiny from the press, Fouchier had backpedaled on his earlier statements about his virus’s lethality. Fauci meanwhile pushed to publish the Fouchier experiment despite biosecurity experts’ concerns the information could fall into the hands of a bioterrorist.
As the question marks suggests, Boffey was skeptical of Fouchier’s assurances. Experts who had read his initial description of the experiment said it stated the airborne virus remained as lethal as the natural one, he wrote. (RELATED: The Fauci Files: Five Explosive Findings Declassified By Tulsi Gabbard)
One sentence really rattled Fauci: “Now, this country’s National Institutes of Health, which financed the research and has its own reputation on the line, is asking the [NSABB] to reconsider its call to redact details before publication.”
“Phil Boffey is really off base here,” Fauci wrote to Collins, on March 4, 2012. “He is acting like a mischievous guy.”
“Clearly, people are getting to Phil Boffey and he is swallowing it,” Fauci sounded off in a more candid email to a subordinate the next morning.
Fauci strongly opposed a recommendation from the NIH’s biosecurity advisors to not publish sensitive details about Fouchier’s experiment. He said that if the advisors did not change their recommendation “the field of research on influenza … has a serious problem.”
“Please delete this e-mail and then delete from the deleted file,” Fauci said on his NIH email in apparent violation of federal record-keeping laws.
Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul highlighted two other instances of Fauci apparently seeking to delete public records in 2020, despite his sworn testimony before another committee in 2024 that he never did.
Fauci ultimately persuaded NIH’s biosecurity advisors to allow the Fouchier experiment to be published in full.
Boffey and Fouchier did not respond to a request for comment.

deduped_items.body_text:
go beyond the headlines.
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
                            Daniel Wollenberg                        
                    August 28, 2026
                        Editor’s note: This is the first article in a new occasional series featuring battles that just didn’t matter, may look important, but in fact had negligible strategic or political effects or were absurd, anticlimactic, or structurally irrelevant to the wars they were part of.
Some battles never end. Their impact is debated endlessly, sometimes for centuries, as they take on new life with new generations of historians and swindlers alike. Few battles better exemplify this eternal lifespan than the Battle of Tours — also known as the Battle of Poitiers — as it was fought between the two cities in modern-day France in October 732 C.E.
The consensus among contemporary historians, such as Franco Cardini, Tomaz Mastnak, and James T. Palmer, is that Tours did not have a major impact on western European history and its significance was blown far out of proportion by subsequent generations. Nonetheless, political discourse, especially on the identitarian far right, insists on Tours’ monumental significance on the fate of Christendom and Europe.
The battle has had an enduring lifespan because of this question of its significance. This “debate” is not quite an academic one between professional historians, but between professional historians who do not think that the battle was crucial and non-specialists with a political agenda who insist that it was. Identitarian nationalists who are not trained historians often argue that the victory of Charles Martel (“the Hammer”) and his Frankish army at Tours halted Muslim incursions into Europe beyond Iberia, thereby “saving” Christian Europe from becoming incorporated into Islamic territory. They go in search of a history that suits their political narratives. The debate about the Battle of Tours, then, is not so much about its historical significance as it is a contest over the legacy and political value of a historical event.
In the lifetime of Muhammad and over the century after his death in 632 C.E., Islam conquered a huge swath of territory across the Middle East, northern Africa, and Iberia with amazing speed, despite the tactics and technology of Muslim armies being roughly the same as those of their adversaries. By the end of the 630s, Muslim forces had conquered Syria and Palestine and were in the process of invading Persia and Egypt. Three decades later, in the 660s, they had swept through the Mediterranean coast and conquered the whole of North Africa. In 711 C.E., a Muslim army of Arabs and Berbers began a campaign of conquest in Iberia and controlled nearly the entire peninsula within a few decades. Incursions into Gaul beginning in the 710s but primarily in the 720s and 730s were part of that campaign of rapid territorial expansion to shore up revenue.
Details about the Battle of Tours in sources at the time are scant and often inaccurate, even if broad outlines of the events are well established. In the years after 711 and the conquering of Iberia, as Berber and Arabic forces attempted to expand their military successes into Gaul, Charles Martel consolidated political and military authority over the Franks in the 720s by securing victories against nearby adversaries like the Saxons and Bavarians.

August 27, 2026
                            
                            Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee                        
                    “Unthreatening and respectful.” That is how the president of the United States described North Korea on Aug. 16, 2026, in his social media post ordering his secretary of defense to scale back joint exercises with South Korea. Two years earlier in Seoul, the U.S.-South Korean alliance agreed that South Korea’s role in an American nuclear operation would involve exercises and training, formalizing those guidelines at a Nuclear Consultative Group meeting co-chaired by Vipin Narang, then-acting assistant secretary of defense for space policy.
Three weeks before the president’s post, on July 24, Narang spoke at the second Deterrence Symposium hosted by South Korea’s Strategic Command. Under the title “Goldilocks of the Nuclear Extended Deterrence,” he delivered a clear diagnosis of South Korea’s nuclear policy. The policies South Korea can pursue, he said, divide broadly into three. Denuclearizing North Korea is for now close to a delusion, and South Korea’s own nuclear armament brings long-term pain and risk, so the optimal policy for meeting North Korea’s advancing nuclear and missile threat is the Goldilocks choice of strengthening American extended deterrence — the “just right” option that avoids both extremes.
Narang then offered a further Goldilocks choice among the options for strengthening extended deterrence, ruling out the redeployment of ground-based tactical nuclear weapons and NATO-style nuclear sharing. The core argument was that forward-deployed nuclear weapons might not be fully usable from an operational standpoint and could divert resources and attention from conventional missions. He offered a sea-based asset as an alternative: the sea-launched cruise missile, a low-yield nuclear cruise missile fired from U.S. Navy submarines.
Read into what Narang excluded, and the underlying premise becomes apparent: The significance of this preference is that a submarine-launched weapon keeps both the operation and delivery of the nuclear asset exclusively in American hands. In other words, Narang’s point is that in the Indo-Pacific, Americans — and Americans only — should fire American nuclear weapons, in sharp contrast to Europe, where NATO allies are assigned the wartime mission of delivering U.S. nuclear weapons under established procedures. The deeper question is how far South Korea’s role should extend in operating and delivering American nuclear weapons, but rather than simply debating whether warheads return to the Korean Peninsula, it also asks why Korea’s role differs from Europe’s.
The reason it is urgent to press this question of nuclear role-sharing is that between North Korea’s conventional provocation and America’s strategic nuclear weapons, particularly at the moment North Korea crosses the threshold with a low-yield tactical weapon, a deterrence gap exists that neither South Korea nor the United States alone can fully cover.
Goldilocks is the main character from a children’s story. Uninvited, a girl enters a home where three bears live. There she finds three bowls of porridge and picks the one that is not too hot, not too cold, but “just right.” She does not set the table. She chooses among bowls someone else has already placed upon it. Logic has a name for the more familiar version of this problem. The “argument to moderation” (argumentum ad temperantiam) is the fallacy of assuming that the midpoint between two extremes is correct, simply because it is the midpoint. Narang’s problem lies in where he set the upper and lower extremes, not in his having chosen the middle.
The metaphor presupposes one more thing: a single ruler. Porridge is ordered by temperature and nothing else. The debate over tactical nuclear redep

                        Editor’s note: This is the first article in a new occasional series featuring battles that just didn’t matter, may look important, but in fact had negligible strategic or political effects or were absurd, anticlimactic, or structurally irrelevant to the wars they were part of.
Some battles never end. Their impact is debated endlessly, sometimes for centuries, as they take on new life with new generations of historians and swindlers alike. Few battles better exemplify this eternal lifespan than the Battle of Tours — also known as the Battle of Poitiers — as it was fought between the two cities in modern-day France in October 732 C.E.
The consensus among contemporary historians, such as Franco Cardini, Tomaz Mastnak, and James T. Palmer, is that Tours did not have a major impact on western European history and its significance was blown far out of proportion by subsequent generations. Nonetheless, political discourse, especially on the identitarian far right, insists on Tours’ monumental significance on the fate of Christendom and Europe.
The battle has had an enduring lifespan because of this question of its significance. This “debate” is not quite an academic one between professional historians, but between professional historians who do not think that the battle was crucial and non-specialists with a political agenda who insist that it was. Identitarian nationalists who are not trained historians often argue that the victory of Charles Martel (“the Hammer”) and his Frankish army at Tours halted Muslim incursions into Europe beyond Iberia, thereby “saving” Christian Europe from becoming incorporated into Islamic territory. They go in search of a history that suits their political narratives. The debate about the Battle of Tours, then, is not so much about its historical significance as it is a contest over the legacy and political value of a historical event.
In the lifetime of Muhammad and over the century after his death in 632 C.E., Islam conquered a huge swath of territory across the Middle East, northern Africa, and Iberia with amazing speed, despite the tactics and technology of Muslim armies being roughly the same as those of their adversaries. By the end of the 630s, Muslim forces had conquered Syria and Palestine and were in the process of invading Persia and Egypt. Three decades later, in the 660s, they had swept through the Mediterranean coast and conquered the whole of North Africa. In 711 C.E., a Muslim army of Arabs and Berbers began a campaign of conquest in Iberia and controlled nearly the entire peninsula within a few decades. Incursions into Gaul beginning in the 710s but primarily in the 720s and 730s were part of that campaign of rapid territorial expansion to shore up revenue.
Details about the Battle of Tours in sources at the time are scant and often inaccurate, even if broad outlines of the events are well established. In the years after 711 and the conquering of Iberia, as Berber and Arabic forces attempted to expand their military successes into Gaul, Charles Martel consolidated political and military authority over the Franks in the 720s by securing victories against nearby adversaries like the Saxons and Bavarians.
Around the same time, the Umayyads, an Arab clan that established the first great Muslim dynasty, raided into Gaul from across the Pyrenees in Spain and besieged and captured the city of Narbonne in 719, were defeated at Toulouse in 721, and then captured the city of Carcassonne in 725. After several years of intermittent raids into Gaul from their base in Narbonne, in 732 C.E., Umayyad forces led by Abd al-Rahmān al-Ghāfiqī, likely motivated by the wealth of its cities, sacked Bordeaux and Poitiers and then move

deduped_items.title: These Local Jails Were Supposed to Detain Immigrants for Only 72 Hours. One Woman Was Held for a Total of 26 Days.
deduped_items.summary: The post These Local Jails Were Supposed to Detain Immigrants for Only 72 Hours. One Woman Was Held for a Total of 26 Days. appeared first on ProPublica.
deduped_items.body_text:
Every third morning Soumia Bensalah was roused before the break of dawn. Pulled from her cell, shackled hand and foot, she was herded onto a bus and driven over Tampa Bay from the Pinellas County Jail to a cramped hold room at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement office.
Each time, she sat there all day, still shackled. Once evening came, she was driven back to the jail, forced to wait for hours in a hallway, photographed, strip-searched, questioned and led back to her cell. This happened five times last December, and Bensalah said it left her exhausted and humiliated.
It was no coincidence that Bensalah, a French Moroccan with a pending green card application, was released from the Pinellas jail and then sent back at regular, 72-hour intervals, according to legal experts. That’s the maximum amount of time that county jails like Pinellas’ can hold immigrants on behalf of ICE. The limit exists to prevent immigrants detained on civil charges from spending too long in jails meant for people detained on criminal charges.
Repeat releases and readmissions, known as rebookings, typically happen in secret and circumvent federal rules and regulations, according to eight legal experts interviewed by ProPublica.
The jail had refused to release the logs that documented Bensalah’s journey, citing federal immigration regulations that shield jail records, which are typically public. We were able to trace the journey after obtaining an unredacted copy of the Pinellas jail’s booking logs from a source who provided them on the condition of anonymity, for fear of workplace reprisal. We checked them against anonymized federal immigration data collected by the Deportation Data Project.
The repeat rebookings stem from the fact that the federal government often doesn’t have enough detention space to jail all the immigrants whom ICE and its cooperating local authorities are rounding up. The shortage of detention space is pronounced in Florida, where the majority of law enforcement agencies have signed agreements to collaborate with ICE on immigration enforcement.
ProPublica’s analysis of data obtained by the Deportation Data Project shows that over the past year, jails in both Pinellas County and in Orange County, Florida, had unusually high numbers of repeat rebookings of immigrants held for ICE compared with other jails nationwide. (Read more about our methodology here.) The Orange County Jail, in Orlando, rebooked 559 of them two or more times from July 2025 until early February 2026, when the data shows the practice ceased. Less than two hours away, in the Tampa Bay area, Pinellas rebooked 174 immigrants at least twice from July 2025 until the practice appeared to cease in July 2026, when zero rebookings were recorded in the data.
The scale in the two Florida counties is unmatched, ProPublica found. Other jails across the country rebooked no more than 10 immigrants two or more times.
All of the rebooked immigrants ProPublica counted were jailed for ICE, meaning they were not being detained on local charges. Our analysis counted a person as having been rebooked only if they cumulatively spent at least 72 hours in jail.
Emily Ryo, a Duke University law professor who studies ICE detention, said jails often can’t provide comprehensive medical screenings, space for confidential legal consultations or even outdoor access. All of those things should be guaranteed to immigrants in ICE custody, according to ICE’s own detention standards.
Two former Department of Homeland Security officials who spoke with ProPublica described the repeated rebookings as an attempt to evade the detention standards.

deduped_items.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
deduped_items.summary: Mourners gather outside the palace as royals, politicians and citizens remember a beloved king, whose son has adopted the family motto "all for norway".
deduped_items.body_text:
Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
- Published
Norwegians, politicians and royals are grieving the death of beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son King Haakon VIII assumes the throne.
After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears.
Hours later, the new king met government ministers for an extraordinary council of state meeting, after which the 53-year-old announced he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".
Harald died peacefully in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after receiving treatment there for a rare blood condition since last week.
The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.
European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".
In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.
Norwegian national footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.
In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.
"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.
"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."
At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.
Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, and headed to the palace.
Norway has declared a period of national mourning until the day of his funeral, which has not yet been announced. Flags will be flown at half-mast, while his portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.
All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding.
King Haakon, who is Harald's younger child, is now the monarch and his wife Mette-Marit queen.
He is due to take an oath before the Norwegian parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service - a stripped-down version of a corronation, which Norway no longer has.
His daughter, the 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, who joined her father to meet ministers at the palace on Friday, is next in line to the throne as crown princess after the rules of succession changed in 1990 to allow firstborn women to inherit the crown.
Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.
Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised.
Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.

deduped_items.title: What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
deduped_items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.
deduped_items.body_text:
What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
Russia's president appears poised to escalate conflict in Eastern Europe
As Russia’s war against Ukraine reaches an inflection point, a conspicuous U.S. intelligence mission to Moscow this week has revealed a fractured debate among allies over Vladimir Putin’s next move.
For weeks now, analysts have speculated that Russia’s strongman president has given up on the notion that U.S. President Donald Trump might be able to coerce Ukraine into meeting his maximalist surrender terms. The thinking is Putin may have decided his five-year war against the country can only be concluded by expanding the conflict.
With Russia’s economy worsening and the pool of volunteers willing to accept a generous paycheque to fight in Ukraine dwindling, Putin could be facing several options.
Ukrainian intelligence officials believe he will soon initiate an unpopular mass mobilization that could send hundreds of thousands of new conscripts into battle, with the goal of overwhelming Ukraine's overstretched defences.
Soldiers from Russia’s poorer regions have made up a disproportionate amount of the fighting force in Ukraine. A country-wide mobilization could draw in men from the more affluent major cities.
Military think-tanks on both sides of the Atlantic have also warned Putin could try to divide Ukraine’s backers in NATO by staging some kind of provocation in Eastern Europe aimed at splitting the alliance.
Presumed and confirmed Russia hybrid attacks across Europe — including attempted assassinations, sabotage and frequent drone incursions — have all intensified of late. But planners remain concerned that Russia could be tempted to seize a slice of Russian-speaking territory in a neighbouring country as a test to see how the alliance would respond.
Russian officials themselves have raised the possibility this week that they could strike directly at Western weapons manufacturers who supply Ukraine, most notably in Great Britain.
Mystery visit
The speculation over Putin’s next move hit a fever pitch earlier this week after the unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Russia.
Rather than slipping into Moscow on a business jet, the standard protocol for clandestine diplomacy, Ratcliffe arrived at Vnukovo airport aboard a massive, highly visible U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster.
Its transponder broadcast the flight path openly across the Atlantic.
U.S. officials appeared to want the world to know Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was significant and that they had something they wanted the Russians to hear clearly.
"It kind of reached a point inside the administration where they said, ‘We need to read the Russians the riot act,'" said Glen Howard with the Saratoga Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based security think-tank with a focus on Ukraine.
But what message was Ratcliffe trying to convey?
Initially, the Wall Street Journal reported the mission was a direct ultimatum to Putin: Back off an escalating grey-zone campaign of hybrid sabotage against NATO's eastern flank or risk triggering a direct allied response.
Military planners have long contemplated whether Putin, in order to get a favourable settlement in Ukraine, might try to draw the United States or NATO directly into the war. Staging a modest attack on a small Baltic nation and testing the Article 5 collective defence provision of the NATO treaty might be one way to do that.
The following day, however, Trump himself appeared to dismiss this, saying he wasn’t worried about a Russian attack on NATO, calling Radcliffe’s trip "semi-routine."
Hours later, the New York Times published an account along the lines of what Trump said that contradicted the earlier reporting. It suggested NATO was not the main topic of the meeting; instead, the warning was for Putin to end his war on Ukraine before Russia’s economic and military situation worsened.
Canada at the front

Hours later, the new king met government ministers for an extraordinary council of state meeting, after which the 53-year-old announced he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".
Harald died peacefully in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after receiving treatment there for a rare blood condition since last week.
The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.
European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".
In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.
Norwegian national footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.
In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.
"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.
"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."
At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.
Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, and headed to the palace.
Norway has declared a period of national mourning until the day of his funeral, which has not yet been announced. Flags will be flown at half-mast, while his portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.

deduped_items.summary: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hoursAustrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from
deduped_items.body_text:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.
Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.
In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”
Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.
MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.
Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.
The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.
A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.
European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.
In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.
This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.
Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.
A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

deduped_items.body_text:
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.
For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.
Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.
Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”
On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.
But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.
For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.
For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.
For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.
None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.
The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.
It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.
Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

deduped_items.title: Right-wing firebrand Milo Yiannopoulos 'detained by ICE at Louisiana airport'
deduped_items.body_text:
Right-wing firebrand Milo Yiannopoulos 'detained by ICE at Louisiana airport'
- Get exclusive reporting, celebrity gossip, sensational photos and more every Tuesday morning in our new Spotlight US newsletter HERE
- Have YOU got a story? Email tips@dailymail.com
- See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Right-wing influencer Milo Yiannopoulos, who used to be Kanye West's chief of staff and is now his publicist, has reportedly been detained by ICE.
Sources claim the British firebrand was taken into custody at an airport in Louisiana, with inmate records indicating he is now at a detention center there, via TMZ.
His reasons for traveling to the state remain unconfirmed, although West is scheduled to perform at the Superdome in New Orleans on Friday.
Since his rise to fame as a political commentator, Yiannopoulos has been a staunch advocate of immigration restriction and mass deportations.
He said in 2017 that he was in America on an O-1 nonimmigrant visa, which is granted to aliens with an 'extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics,' per the US Citizenship and Immigration Services policy manual.
The Daily Mail has contacted Yiannopoulos and ICE for comment.
Right-wing influencer Milo Yiannopoulos, who used to be Kanye West's chief of staff and is now his publicist, has reportedly been detained by ICE; pictured 2024
West is pictured with Yiannopoulos in Beverly Hills in November 2022, the same month they visited Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago with Nick fuentes in tow
O-1 visas, which require sponsorship by an 'agent' or employer, can also be given to individuals of 'extraordinary achievement' in movies and TV.
Yiannopoulos enjoys a longstanding association with West and acted as director of political operations on his 2024 US presidential campaign.
In 2022, during his time as West's political honcho, he helped arrange the rapper's explosively controversial Mar-a-Lago summit with Donald Trump and the self-described 'white identitarian' streaming star Nick Fuentes.
Yiannopoulous has since dramatically fallen out with Fuentes, whom he now relentlessly derides on X, formerly known as Twitter.
In 2017, he exchanged vows in Hawaii with a black man whom he publicly referred to only as 'John,' otherwise carefully concealing his identity.
As such, it remains unconfirmed whether Yiannopoulos became eligible to obtain American citizenship or a green card via marriage to a US national.
Yiannopoulos has characterized himself as 'ex-gay' since 2021, and has commenced divorce proceedings with his husband.
His reported ICE woes come after his client, West, was banned from Yiannopoulos' native Britain over the antisemitic diatribes that torpedoed his career, including praise for Hitler and a vow to go 'death con 3 on JEWISH PEOPLE.'
Sources claim the British firebrand was taken into custody at an airport in Louisiana, with inmate records indicating he is now at a detention center there, via TMZ; pictured 2017
West took out a full-page ad apologizing for the comments in the Wall Street Journal this January, three months before he was prohibited from entering the UK.
He had been scheduled to a headline a music festival at Finsbury Park in London that was called off altogether after his appearance there became impossible.
West has also seen planned concerts canceled in Poland and France this year as a result of the continuing backlash to his tirades about Jews, as well as to a past embrace of Nazi iconography so extravagant that he released a single called Heil Hitler and sold merchandise splashed with swastikas.
He was set to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg in October, which would have made him the highest-profile western artist to play Russia since the outbreak of the Ukraine War, but those shows were also scrapped amid blowback.
However he has been able to stage concerts in America, as well as in Mexico, Turkey and such post-Soviet countries as Georgia and Kazakhstan.

deduped_items.title: Should William be 'the bigger man' and extend an olive branch to Harry? 'Absolute rubbish', says REBECCA ENGLISH, telling Palace Confidential she would 'personally applaud' the Prince of Wales if he NEVER reconciled with his brother
deduped_items.body_text:
- WATCH: 'BAFFLING!' Have Harry & Meghan ALREADY compromised their own UK security?
- LISTEN: Why Now? Inside Harry and Meghan's Return to Britain - Listen to the latest Daily Mail Deep Dive podcast
- See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Those calling for Prince William to do the legwork in patching up the relationship with his brother Harry are spouting 'absolute rubbish', Rebecca English has told Palace Confidential.
Speaking to a panel of experts, the Daily Mail's Royal Editor said she had been angered by recent comments calling on the Prince of Wales to 'be the bigger man' and reach out to his brother now that he is back in Britain.
She argued that Harry's behaviour since Megxit was 'nasty' and 'vindictive' enough to warrant estrangement, and that William should not be judged if he chooses not to seek reconciliation.
Harry, Meghan and their children touched down in Birmingham by private jet on Wednesday, before heading for the Cotswolds, where Archie and Lilibet are due to start school in September.
Those calling for Prince William to do the legwork in patching up the relationship with his brother Harry are spouting 'absolute rubbish', Rebecca English has told Palace Confidential
English argued that Harry's behaviour since Megxit was 'nasty' and 'vindictive' enough to warrant estrangement
The brothers did not meet during Harry's last visit to Britain in July. They have reportedly not spoken since the late Queen's funeral in September 2022.
'It makes me so angry', English said.
'I am not speaking here as a royal journalist, I am speaking from a personal perspective. This whole mounting agenda from certain people, who say it's time that William be the bigger man and extend an olive branch. I say it's absolute rubbish.
'It's very difficult to extract the professional from the personal. Harry has made this all so vindictive, nasty and bitter that it's impossible to separate the two.
'If William decides not to reconcile with his brother, then that is entirely his choice, and he should, I would say, be personally applauded for it.
'If a sibling had done to me what Harry has done to William, in terms of attacking him personally, his wife, his family and the institution he works for, I would never speak to them again.
'I just think people should understand and respect William's decision on that.'
Elsewhere in the show, the conversation turned to whether Harry and Meghan are entitled to taxpayer funded security now that they are living in the UK again.
The Prince lost a Court of Appeal challenge over his police protection in May 2025. His security had been downgraded in 2020 after he stepped back as a working royal and moved abroad, with his absence from Britain central to that decision.
After that ruling, Harry said he could not envisage a world in which he would bring his wife and children back to his homeland because of the security risk.
Elsewhere in the show, the conversation turned to whether Harry and Meghan are entitled to taxpayer funded security now that they are living in the UK again
Ailsa Anderson, the late Queen's former press secretary, warned that any move to hand the couple full taxpayer funded protection would provoke fury, pointing to families struggling with the rising cost of living.
But the Daily Mail's Editor-at-Large Alison Boshoff argued that although such a decision will be unpopular, the threats Harry faces as a royal and a veteran are real enough to warrant protection.
'It's not a popularity contest', she argued.
'If you need security, you get it… I know people are genuinely angry, but actually, does he need it? I think he clearly does. As a former serviceman and someone in his position.
'I agree that it seems unfair and really enraging. However, I would say that issue is coming down the pipe and Buckingham Palace and everyone else is going to have to find some way to sell it to the public.'
Watch the full episode now by subscribing to Palace Confidential on YouTube.

deduped_items.title: Welcome to the dystopian future of Test cricket
deduped_items.summary: England are on course to hammer Pakistan again, but the margin of victory does nothing more than to illustrate the global game's growing problem
deduped_items.body_text:
Day 2: England 290 and 81-3 (Shahzad 2-26) lead Pakistan 110 (Robinson 4-11, Archer 3-26) by 261 runs
LORD’S — As well as England bowled on day two of this second Test, by the time they routed Pakistan for 110 to establish a first-innings lead of 180 you were left feeling that perhaps this was a glimpse into a dystopian future for the sport’s oldest format.
Test cricket has been written off for much of its 150-year history. But as Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer tormented Pakistan’s batting line-up at Lord’s, the charade that this was actually a proper contest evaporated. We all knew the result at this point, even if England tried to keep things interesting by losing a couple of early wickets in their second innings.
Sport without consequence is boring. So more mismatches like this really do threaten to kill off Test cricket.
Bangladesh were rightly lauded for their landmark win against the Australians in Darwin earlier this month. But it’s the fact these results are so rare that makes them so newsworthy.
Many fear that in the near future only matches between England, Australia and India will be either competitive or meaningful.
Joe Root won’t care – for now
Pakistan are bad. We know this. Last week’s two-and-a-half-day innings walkover for England at Headingley told us that much.
But at what point does Test cricket cease to be watchable?
Joe Root, in his second match back as captain, will not care. England have not won a series since December 2024 and in a week where the team’s off-field issues came to the fore yet again, another one-sided victory will be manna from heaven.
Nor will Robinson, whose haul of four for 11 from 13 overs at an economy rate of 0.84, was the latest chapter of a remarkable summer where he has taken 19 wickets in three Tests at 8.84.
Jofra Archer, who hit close to 95 miles per hour on a day when he took three wickets, was sensational. As was Josh Tongue, whose two for 27 took his total in this current World Test Championship cycle to 55. Only Australia’s Mitchell Starc has more.
England are building a bowling attack to be excited about as we head into next summer’s home Ashes series.
But what are they up against? Take nothing away from the skill and hard work of England’s bowlers. Nor the efforts of the batters.
But they have been given perhaps the perfect opponents to face following a summer of upheaval.
Mismatches such as last week’s in Leeds and are the current debacle at Lord’s do not bode well for the future.
Pakistan are their own special case given the dysfunction at the top of their own board.
The real reason Test cricket is dying
Yet the economic imbalance in the world game right now means that regardless of how incompetent or not individual boards are, they will always be struggling to keep their Test teams competitive. That’s because odds are stacked too far in favour of the “Big Three” of England, Australia and India, who take around 53 per cent of the £468m distributed annually by the International Cricket Council. India’s share of that is almost 40 per cent.
Their individual broadcast deals – the England & Wales Cricket Board’s current one with Sky is worth £220m a year – are even more significant for two reasons.
Many countries struggle to get viable deals at all and so actually lose money hosting Test cricket – unless it’s against India, the biggest draw in the world. They also struggle to pay their top players decent central contracts, meaning the best are incentivised to play franchise cricket rather than for their nations.
	
Read more
- Chris Stocks: England have been shown how to bat properly again
- Vernon Philander: I taught Ollie Robinson to bowl slower – England are so wrong about pace
So teams outside the “Big Three” end up playing less Test cricket and lose the services of their most talented players. This will only get worse as the franchise world gets bigger and more lucrative.
England’s top centrally-contracted players earn around £1.5m a year. It means someone like Harry B

deduped_items.title: عراقچی: نهضت خونخواهی رهبر شهید ادامه خواهد داشت
deduped_items.summary: تهران- ایرنا- سید عباس عراقچی وزیر امور خارجه جمهوری اسلامی ایران با تأکید بر اینکه شهادت رهبر انقلاب پس از ۷۰ سال مجاهدت بی‌چشم‌داشت، نهضت جدیدی از خونخواهی و ایستادگی را رقم زده است، گفت: همان‌گونه که نهضت خون سیدالشهدا(ع) پس از بیش از ۱۴۰۰ سال ادامه دارد، نهضت خونخواهی رهبر شهید نیز ادامه خواهد یافت و ملت ایران در برابر هرگونه تجاوز، زیاده‌خواهی و فشار دشمنان، با تکیه بر استقلال، توانمندی داخلی و حفظ عزت خود ایستادگی خواهد کرد.

deduped_items.summary: تهران- ایرنا- سید عباس عراقچی وزیر امور خارجه جمهوری اسلامی ایران با تأکید بر اینکه شهادت رهبر انقلاب پس از ۷۰ سال مجاهدت بی‌چشم‌داشت، نهضت جدیدی از خونخواهی و ایستادگی را رقم زده است، گفت: همان‌گونه که نهضت خون سیدالشهدا(ع) پس از بیش از ۱۴۰۰ سال ادامه دارد، نهضت خونخواهی رهبر شهید نیز ادامه خواهد یافت و ملت ایران در برابر هرگونه تجاوز، زیاده‌خواهی و فشار دشمنان، با تکیه بر استقلال، توانمندی داخلی و حفظ عزت خود ایستادگی خواهد کرد.

deduped_items.summary: احمد دنیامالی، وزیر ورزش دولت جمهوری اسلامی درباره معرفی نشدن چادرملو به عنوان نماینده فوتبال ایران در لیگ قهرمانان آسیا گفت: «داریم فکر می‌کنیم حتما فرصتی را برای این باشگاه، برای فصل آینده ایجاد کنیم، هنوز به نتیجه نرسیده‌ایم، در حد یک پیشنهاد است. من در حال تلاش برای آن هستم.»

deduped_items.title: As Iran Threatens Radio Farda And Other Media, US Points To Tehran's Record Of Targeting Journalists
deduped_items.summary: The US said it was aware of threats by Iran's armed forces to put Persian-language media outlets including RFE/RL's Radio Farda on a list of potential military targets, and pointed to what it said was Tehran's record of harassment and attempted attacks against journalists and dissidents abroad.
deduped_items.body_text:
WASHINGTON -- The United States said it was aware of threats by Iran's armed forces to put Persian-language media outlets including RFE/RL's Radio Farda on a list of potential military targets, and pointed to what it said was Tehran's record of harassment and attempted attacks against journalists and dissidents abroad.
In an August 28 response to a query from RFE/RL, a State Department spokesperson said, "We are aware of these reports."
"The Iranian regime has repeatedly harassed and attempted to kidnap and kill journalists and Iranian dissidents worldwide simply for exercising their freedoms. This is longstanding, despicable behavior from a regime that has propagated terror globally for decades," the spokesperson said.
"The United States stands with innocent civilians targeted by Iran and continues working with allies and partners to expose these threats, share threat information, and hold perpetrators accountable," the spokesperson continued.
In a televised interview earlier this week, Iranian armed forces spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi named Radio Farda, Iran International, BBC Persian, and Manoto, and said their employees could be included in Iran's "bank of military targets." He called them "soldiers of Zionism and criminal America" and claimed, without providing evidence, that the outlets were connected variously to the CIA, Mossad, and other foreign intelligence services.
David Kramer, executive director of the George W. Bush Institute and a former US assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights, and labor, said Tehran's warning reflected the importance of the media outlets it said could be targeted.
"It's not a surprise that the Iranian regime would view outlets like Radio Farda and BBC Persian-language service as threats, since they don't want the Iranian people to know what's really happening," Kramer told RFE/RL.
"The regime's reaction shows that these services have a real impact inside Iran, whereas the regime prefers to operate through silence and violence against its own people and its neighbors," he said.
Radio Farda is the Iranian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), which says its mission is to "promote democratic values by providing accurate, uncensored news and open debate in countries where a free press is threatened and disinformation is pervasive."
Kramer said the media outlets "must be protected to be able to do their important work in advancing the interests of the American people through soft power, while also letting the Iranian people know they are not forgotten."
The Czech Republic, which hosts RFE/RL and Radio Farda in Prague, has protested the threats. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka said he was summoning the Iranian ambassador to appear at the ministry over the matter, Czech media reported.
"Radio Farda, based in Prague, has been one of the few channels getting verified information to the Iranian population. Its importance was especially clear during the mass repression which the Iranian regime subjected its people to in the winter," Czech Foreign Ministry spokesman Adam Corgo told Czech Radio.
He was referring to a deadly crackdown on nationwide protests in Iran in January. Foreign-based Iranian rights groups say they have verified around 7,000 deaths but that the real death toll is likely higher.
Thomas Melia, a former senior State Department official focusing on human rights and now a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Democracy and Civil Society, said the threat should be taken seriously. He said Radio Farda personnel in Prague and elsewhere "need to heighten their security awareness," pointing to the Iranian state's actions targeting dissidents abroad.
Melia also said Tehran's threat underscored the importance of Radio Farda's work.

deduped_items.title: South Africa freedom day memorial gathering reveals its pursuit of dignity and inclusive governance in post apartheid era
deduped_items.body_text:
IN-DEPTH / IN-DEPTH
                        South Africa freedom day memorial gathering reveals its pursuit of dignity and inclusive governance in post apartheid era
                        Politics finds its rhythm
                        
                     Editor's Note: 
In an era of profound global shifts and increasingly complex regional dynamics, a proper understanding of the world must be rooted in "grounded experience" and localized insights. Global Times English edition, in collaboration with the Academy of International and Regional Communication Studies, Communication University of China, is proud to launch "Local Insights," an English-language column dedicated to original, field-based observations.
We invite Chinese scholars and professionals who are studying, conducting exchanges, or working outside China, as well as international students and friends living and studying in China who are familiar with the social contexts of their home countries or third countries, to begin from first-hand field experience and engage with social, cultural, and contemporary issues beyond China. In the fifth article of this column, drawing on her onâtheâground experience as a Chinese exchange scholar, the author observes a South Africa Freedom Day memorial gathering, revealing how local politics unfolds through collective singing, dancing, and grassroots participation, while also reflecting on the gap between political liberation and economic justice.
As a PhD student, I am currently on an exchange program at Nelson Mandela University in South Africa, with support from the China Scholarship Council. Since arriving here, I have developed a habit of stepping beyond campus whenever possible. Community meetings, municipal events and public gatherings have become a vital way for me to engage with local life. This time, a local friend recommended that I attend a memorial event in Kariega, organized by the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) in honor of its former president, Phumzile John Gomomo. Beyond that, I had little sense of what kind of gathering I was about to enter.
It was on the way that I noticed the streets were unusually vibrant. Groups of people were dressed in colorful attire, with bright Xhosa headscarves and garments bearing political symbols. My friend then reminded me that it was April 27, which is Freedom Day in South Africa. On this day in 1994, South Africa held its first non-racial election, formally ending apartheid and inaugurating democratic rule. Over the past three decades, Freedom Day commemorates political liberation, while also inviting recurring reflection on whether the promise of freedom has been fully realized. In that sense, Freedom Day marks an important moment for observing contemporary South African politics and social sentiment.
The aerial view of Johannesburg, South Africa Photo: VCG
From street to hall: Entering Freedom Day
The event was scheduled to begin at 10 am, and we arrived shortly before the hour. Yet there were not many people present. Banners of COSATU, the South African Communist Party (SACP), and the African National Congress (ANC) had already been displayed inside the hall, quietly framing the political context of the gathering. Although my understanding was still limited, I could already sense that their presence mattered. COSATU, SACP and ANC represent key forces in South Africa's political landscape, historically linked through the "Tripartite Alliance" formed during the anti-apartheid struggle and sustained in various forms since 1994. I could see that this was not simply a local gathering, but one embedded within a much longer political tradition.
What struck me first was how different the atmosphere was from what I had expected of a political gathering. There was no sense of urgency or visible tension.
