deduped_items.title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return
deduped_items.summary: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disasterFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastThe families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster manageme
deduped_items.body_text:
The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.
Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday that the total number of people missing had risen sharply to more than 1,900 swelled by 933 workers on hydropower projects on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning. The number of people killed is at least 584.
One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.
Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.
“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.
“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”
Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.
Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.
“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”
Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.
The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.
“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.
“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.
“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”
Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.
“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”
Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.
Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.
“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”
Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.
He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.
Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.
Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Spri

deduped_items.title: What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
deduped_items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.
deduped_items.body_text:
What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
Russia's president appears poised to escalate conflict in Eastern Europe
As Russia’s war against Ukraine reaches an inflection point, a conspicuous U.S. intelligence mission to Moscow this week has revealed a fractured debate among allies over Vladimir Putin’s next move.
For weeks now, analysts have speculated that Russia’s strongman president has given up on the notion that U.S. President Donald Trump might be able to coerce Ukraine into meeting his maximalist surrender terms. The thinking is Putin may have decided his five-year war against the country can only be concluded by expanding the conflict.
With Russia’s economy worsening and the pool of volunteers willing to accept a generous paycheque to fight in Ukraine dwindling, Putin could be facing several options.
Ukrainian intelligence officials believe he will soon initiate an unpopular mass mobilization that could send hundreds of thousands of new conscripts into battle, with the goal of overwhelming Ukraine's overstretched defences.
Soldiers from Russia’s poorer regions have made up a disproportionate amount of the fighting force in Ukraine. A country-wide mobilization could draw in men from the more affluent major cities.
Military think-tanks on both sides of the Atlantic have also warned Putin could try to divide Ukraine’s backers in NATO by staging some kind of provocation in Eastern Europe aimed at splitting the alliance.
Presumed and confirmed Russia hybrid attacks across Europe — including attempted assassinations, sabotage and frequent drone incursions — have all intensified of late. But planners remain concerned that Russia could be tempted to seize a slice of Russian-speaking territory in a neighbouring country as a test to see how the alliance would respond.
Russian officials themselves have raised the possibility this week that they could strike directly at Western weapons manufacturers who supply Ukraine, most notably in Great Britain.
Mystery visit
The speculation over Putin’s next move hit a fever pitch earlier this week after the unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Russia.
Rather than slipping into Moscow on a business jet, the standard protocol for clandestine diplomacy, Ratcliffe arrived at Vnukovo airport aboard a massive, highly visible U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster.
Its transponder broadcast the flight path openly across the Atlantic.
U.S. officials appeared to want the world to know Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was significant and that they had something they wanted the Russians to hear clearly.
"It kind of reached a point inside the administration where they said, ‘We need to read the Russians the riot act,'" said Glen Howard with the Saratoga Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based security think-tank with a focus on Ukraine.
But what message was Ratcliffe trying to convey?
Initially, the Wall Street Journal reported the mission was a direct ultimatum to Putin: Back off an escalating grey-zone campaign of hybrid sabotage against NATO's eastern flank or risk triggering a direct allied response.
Military planners have long contemplated whether Putin, in order to get a favourable settlement in Ukraine, might try to draw the United States or NATO directly into the war. Staging a modest attack on a small Baltic nation and testing the Article 5 collective defence provision of the NATO treaty might be one way to do that.
The following day, however, Trump himself appeared to dismiss this, saying he wasn’t worried about a Russian attack on NATO, calling Radcliffe’s trip "semi-routine."
Hours later, the New York Times published an account along the lines of what Trump said that contradicted the earlier reporting. It suggested NATO was not the main topic of the meeting; instead, the warning was for Putin to end his war on Ukraine before Russia’s economic and military situation worsened.

deduped_items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.
deduped_items.body_text:
What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
Russia's president appears poised to escalate conflict in Eastern Europe
As Russia’s war against Ukraine reaches an inflection point, a conspicuous U.S. intelligence mission to Moscow this week has revealed a fractured debate among allies over Vladimir Putin’s next move.
For weeks now, analysts have speculated that Russia’s strongman president has given up on the notion that U.S. President Donald Trump might be able to coerce Ukraine into meeting his maximalist surrender terms. The thinking is Putin may have decided his five-year war against the country can only be concluded by expanding the conflict.
With Russia’s economy worsening and the pool of volunteers willing to accept a generous paycheque to fight in Ukraine dwindling, Putin could be facing several options.
Ukrainian intelligence officials believe he will soon initiate an unpopular mass mobilization that could send hundreds of thousands of new conscripts into battle, with the goal of overwhelming Ukraine's overstretched defences.
Soldiers from Russia’s poorer regions have made up a disproportionate amount of the fighting force in Ukraine. A country-wide mobilization could draw in men from the more affluent major cities.
Military think-tanks on both sides of the Atlantic have also warned Putin could try to divide Ukraine’s backers in NATO by staging some kind of provocation in Eastern Europe aimed at splitting the alliance.
Presumed and confirmed Russia hybrid attacks across Europe — including attempted assassinations, sabotage and frequent drone incursions — have all intensified of late. But planners remain concerned that Russia could be tempted to seize a slice of Russian-speaking territory in a neighbouring country as a test to see how the alliance would respond.
Russian officials themselves have raised the possibility this week that they could strike directly at Western weapons manufacturers who supply Ukraine, most notably in Great Britain.
Mystery visit
The speculation over Putin’s next move hit a fever pitch earlier this week after the unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Russia.
Rather than slipping into Moscow on a business jet, the standard protocol for clandestine diplomacy, Ratcliffe arrived at Vnukovo airport aboard a massive, highly visible U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster.
Its transponder broadcast the flight path openly across the Atlantic.
U.S. officials appeared to want the world to know Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was significant and that they had something they wanted the Russians to hear clearly.
"It kind of reached a point inside the administration where they said, ‘We need to read the Russians the riot act,'" said Glen Howard with the Saratoga Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based security think-tank with a focus on Ukraine.
But what message was Ratcliffe trying to convey?
Initially, the Wall Street Journal reported the mission was a direct ultimatum to Putin: Back off an escalating grey-zone campaign of hybrid sabotage against NATO's eastern flank or risk triggering a direct allied response.
Military planners have long contemplated whether Putin, in order to get a favourable settlement in Ukraine, might try to draw the United States or NATO directly into the war. Staging a modest attack on a small Baltic nation and testing the Article 5 collective defence provision of the NATO treaty might be one way to do that.
The following day, however, Trump himself appeared to dismiss this, saying he wasn’t worried about a Russian attack on NATO, calling Radcliffe’s trip "semi-routine."
Hours later, the New York Times published an account along the lines of what Trump said that contradicted the earlier reporting. It suggested NATO was not the main topic of the meeting; instead, the warning was for Putin to end his war on Ukraine before Russia’s economic and military situation worsened.

deduped_items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.
deduped_items.body_text:
What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
Russia's president appears poised to escalate conflict in Eastern Europe
As Russia’s war against Ukraine reaches an inflection point, a conspicuous U.S. intelligence mission to Moscow this week has revealed a fractured debate among allies over Vladimir Putin’s next move.
For weeks now, analysts have speculated that Russia’s strongman president has given up on the notion that U.S. President Donald Trump might be able to coerce Ukraine into meeting his maximalist surrender terms. The thinking is Putin may have decided his five-year war against the country can only be concluded by expanding the conflict.
With Russia’s economy worsening and the pool of volunteers willing to accept a generous paycheque to fight in Ukraine dwindling, Putin could be facing several options.
Ukrainian intelligence officials believe he will soon initiate an unpopular mass mobilization that could send hundreds of thousands of new conscripts into battle, with the goal of overwhelming Ukraine's overstretched defences.
Soldiers from Russia’s poorer regions have made up a disproportionate amount of the fighting force in Ukraine. A country-wide mobilization could draw in men from the more affluent major cities.
Military think-tanks on both sides of the Atlantic have also warned Putin could try to divide Ukraine’s backers in NATO by staging some kind of provocation in Eastern Europe aimed at splitting the alliance.
Presumed and confirmed Russia hybrid attacks across Europe — including attempted assassinations, sabotage and frequent drone incursions — have all intensified of late. But planners remain concerned that Russia could be tempted to seize a slice of Russian-speaking territory in a neighbouring country as a test to see how the alliance would respond.
Russian officials themselves have raised the possibility this week that they could strike directly at Western weapons manufacturers who supply Ukraine, most notably in Great Britain.
Mystery visit
The speculation over Putin’s next move hit a fever pitch earlier this week after the unusual visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Russia.
Rather than slipping into Moscow on a business jet, the standard protocol for clandestine diplomacy, Ratcliffe arrived at Vnukovo airport aboard a massive, highly visible U.S. Air Force C-17 Globemaster.
Its transponder broadcast the flight path openly across the Atlantic.
U.S. officials appeared to want the world to know Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow was significant and that they had something they wanted the Russians to hear clearly.
"It kind of reached a point inside the administration where they said, ‘We need to read the Russians the riot act,'" said Glen Howard with the Saratoga Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based security think-tank with a focus on Ukraine.
But what message was Ratcliffe trying to convey?
Initially, the Wall Street Journal reported the mission was a direct ultimatum to Putin: Back off an escalating grey-zone campaign of hybrid sabotage against NATO's eastern flank or risk triggering a direct allied response.
Military planners have long contemplated whether Putin, in order to get a favourable settlement in Ukraine, might try to draw the United States or NATO directly into the war. Staging a modest attack on a small Baltic nation and testing the Article 5 collective defence provision of the NATO treaty might be one way to do that.
The following day, however, Trump himself appeared to dismiss this, saying he wasn’t worried about a Russian attack on NATO, calling Radcliffe’s trip "semi-routine."
Hours later, the New York Times published an account along the lines of what Trump said that contradicted the earlier reporting. It suggested NATO was not the main topic of the meeting; instead, the warning was for Putin to end his war on Ukraine before Russia’s economic and military situation worsened.

deduped_items.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
deduped_items.summary: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hoursAustrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from
deduped_items.body_text:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.
Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.
In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”
Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.
MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.
Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.
The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.
A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.
European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.
In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.
This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.
Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.
A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

deduped_items.body_text:
'All of a sudden the rug was pulled out': How Coyote vs. Acme went from the shelf to the big screen
In 2022, the cast and crew of Coyote vs. Acme attended a “funeral screening.”
It was as grim as it sounds. Warner Bros. had already announced the finished film was going to be forever shelved. Studio execs had controversially decided to take a $30-million tax writeoff as a cost-saving exercise rather than take on the expense of releasing and distributing it.
The film’s stars, Will Forte and Lana Condor, were among those went to the screening. The mood was not jubilant, to say the least, even though everyone was impressed with what they saw on the screen.
“That experience of watching the film was very layered,” says Condor, in a Zoom interview with Postmedia alongside Forte. “We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘”
“The shoot went great, we had been hearing the post-process was great, they were already testing it and the testing was going great,” adds Forte. “All of a sudden the rug was pulled out.”
“And so then when we watched the film and the credits rolled, there was this mass confusion and anger,” Condor says. “When credits rolled, we were like ‘This is a great movie! How is this possible?’”
After facing significant backlash and negative media coverage, the studio execs changed their minds and allowed an outside distributor to purchase the film. Enter Ketchup Entertainment, an independent film company that picked it up and held another screening before its wide release on Aug. 28.
The feeling was different the second time around.
“That was a great watch because we knew it was going to come out and it’s a great movie,” Condor says.
This strange chapter in the film’s behind-the-scenes story is being seen by some commentators as an indictment of the tone-deaf corporate indifference that seems to have overrun Hollywood studios these days. It is also strangely fitting for the tone of Coyote Vs. Acme, a story about corporate indifference and underdogs who never give up. Further vindication has come from early reviews, which have been largely positive. “Consistently funny and clever” proclaimed Brian Tallerico of rogerebert.com. “A cracking comedy that’s easily among the top ‘Looney Tunes’ movies ever,” writes Johnny Oleksinksi in the New York Post. “It’s smart, silly, and ultimately inspiring,” says Kristy Puchko of Mashable.com.
Directed by Dave Green and based on a satirical 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs. Acme blends animation and live-action in the spirit of Who Framed Roger Rabbit? Its central plot revolves around Wile E. Coyote’s decision to sue Acme, the massive corporation behind the endless trail of shoddy equipment he has used in his tireless pursuit of the Road Runner. He enlists the sad-eyed and defeated Kevin Avery (Forte) to represent him, an ambulance-chasing lawyer who specializes in getting small, out-of-court settlements from Acme for cartoon characters.
Avery is joined by his idealistic niece, Paige (played by Condor), who possesses unyielding enthusiasm and optimism for the case even though it pits them against a behemoth and heartless corporation fronted by a ruthless lawyer (played by former pro-wrestler Jon Cena).
“That experience of watching the film was very layered. We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘
The mute Coyote shifts from the antagonist of the Looney Tunes shorts to a somewhat sympathetic character whose steadfast belief in his own genius despite years of failure becomes the endearing centre of the film. What follows is a story about friendship, loyalty and perseverance filled with slapstick humour, heart and appearances by a long line of Looney Tunes favourites. That includes everything from significant roles for Foghorn Leghorn and Tweety Bird to savvy bits featuring cameos by Pepe Le Pew, Gossamer and Dr. Lorre.

In 2022, the cast and crew of Coyote vs. Acme attended a “funeral screening.”
It was as grim as it sounds. Warner Bros. had already announced the finished film was going to be forever shelved. Studio execs had controversially decided to take a $30-million tax writeoff as a cost-saving exercise rather than take on the expense of releasing and distributing it.
The film’s stars, Will Forte and Lana Condor, were among those went to the screening. The mood was not jubilant, to say the least, even though everyone was impressed with what they saw on the screen.
“That experience of watching the film was very layered,” says Condor, in a Zoom interview with Postmedia alongside Forte. “We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘”
“The shoot went great, we had been hearing the post-process was great, they were already testing it and the testing was going great,” adds Forte. “All of a sudden the rug was pulled out.”
“And so then when we watched the film and the credits rolled, there was this mass confusion and anger,” Condor says. “When credits rolled, we were like ‘This is a great movie! How is this possible?’”
After facing significant backlash and negative media coverage, the studio execs changed their minds and allowed an outside distributor to purchase the film. Enter Ketchup Entertainment, an independent film company that picked it up and held another screening before its wide release on Aug. 28.

deduped_items.title: Murió Carnicero de Bosnia en La Haya
deduped_items.summary: El ex jefe militar de los serbios de Bosnia y criminal de guerra Ratko Mladic, condenado a cadena perpetua por la justicia internacional y apodado El carnicero de Bosnia por su papel en la matanza de Srebrenica, murió ayer a los 84 años en La Haya. El deceso lo confirmó el mecanismo residual internacional de los tribunales penales de Naciones Unidas en La Haya, tras añadir que la jueza uruguaya Graciela Gatti Santana ordenó “una investigación exhaustiva sobre las circunstancias” de su muerte. deduped_items.title: Trump anuncia la creación de una academia espacial para formar a las futuras generaciones
deduped_items.summary: El líder estadounidense impulsa una academia espacial para formar expertos en un sector en auge, ligada a la NASA y la industria civil.Astronautas del programa Artemis II son honrados tras completar un vuelo lunar histórico, destacando la colaboración internacional en la misión.
deduped_items.body_text:
El presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, anunció este viernes la creación de la Academia Espacial de Estados Unidos para capacitar y formar a las futuras generaciones de profesionales del sector, en plena expansión del programa espacial.
"En unos momentos firmaré una orden ejecutiva para comenzar el proceso de creación de una nueva academia nacional: la Academia Espacial de EE.UU. (...) Ahora tendremos una academia para la Fuerza Espacial, la NASA y la industria espacial civil", dijo el mandatario durante un acto en el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA en Houston (Texas).
Trump viajó a Texas para condecorar con la Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso a los cuatro astronautas de la misión Artemis II, que en abril completaron el primer sobrevuelo tripulado alrededor de la Luna en más de 50 años.
Según la orden ejecutiva firmada por el presidente, la academia no solo educará a astronautas, sino también a científicos, ingenieros, operadores, empresarios, funcionarios públicos y combatientes.
Los alumnos que se gradúen estarán obligados a servir un tiempo en las Fuerzas Armadas o en la NASA.
Sin embargo, el documento no dio detalles sobre el futuro emplazamiento de la academia.
Este anuncio trasciende en un momento de gran actividad espacial en Estados Unidos, no solo por parte de la NASA, sino procedente de empresas privadas como SpaceX o Blue Origin, entre otras.
Una de las metas a corto plazo de la NASA es devolver al ser humano a la Luna a través del programa Artemis, y posteriormente crear un asentamiento humano permanente en el satélite que facilite el salto a Marte.
Los astronautas de la NASA Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover y Christina Koch, además de su compañero de la Agencia Espacial Canadiense (CSA) Jeremy Hansen, jugaron un papel muy importante en ese objetivo el pasado abril, cuando completaron el primer sobrevuelo tripulado alrededor de la Luna en más de 50 años en el marco de Artemis II.
Por su papel durante esa expedición, los cuatro astronautas recibieron este viernes la máxima distinción que el Gobierno de Estados Unidos otorga a astronautas, científicos o personal de aviación por sus servicios relacionados con el programa espacial.
Los astronautas despegaron a bordo de la cápsula Orión el pasado 1 de abril desde las instalaciones de la NASA en Cabo Cañaveral y regresaron a la Tierra el 10 de abril.

Los astronautas despegaron a bordo de la cápsula Orión el pasado 1 de abril desde las instalaciones de la NASA en Cabo Cañaveral y regresaron a la Tierra el 10 de abril.

Irán se muestra abierto a la reabrir el diálogo con Estados Unidos para poner fin a la guerra y llama a levantar la presión: 'No es imposible'
Los esfuerzos diplomáticos han intentado durante meses poner fin definitivo a la guerra iniciada por Washington e Israel el 28 de febrero, sin éxito.
Irán dejó abierta la puerta a la diplomacia este viernes, justo seis meses después del inicio de la guerra con Estados Unidos, pero solo si Washington abandona su campaña de presión.

Irán se muestra abierto a la reabrir el diálogo con Estados Unidos para poner fin a la guerra y llama a levantar la presión: 'No es imposible'
Los esfuerzos diplomáticos han intentado durante meses poner fin definitivo a la guerra iniciada por Washington e Israel el 28 de febrero, sin éxito.
Irán dejó abierta la puerta a la diplomacia este viernes, justo seis meses después del inicio de la guerra con Estados Unidos, pero solo si Washington abandona su campaña de presión.
"Retomar la diplomacia no es imposible. Depende de que Estados Unidos comprenda un hecho sencillo: la presión no funciona", escribió en X el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores iraní, Abás Araqchi.
Los esfuerzos diplomáticos, liderados por mediadores como Pakistán y Catar, han intentado durante meses poner fin definitivo a la guerra iniciada por Estados Unidos e Israel el 28 de febrero, sin éxito.
Si bien en abril se acordó un alto el fuego y en junio se firmó un memorando de entendimiento para un acuerdo de paz definitivo, no se ha alcanzado ningún acuerdo y Washington ha declarado desde entonces una "guerra económica" contra Teherán.
En un nuevo intento por revitalizar la diplomacia, Araqchi se entrevistó con su homólogo catarí el jueves en Teherán para hablar del estrecho de Ormuz, cerrado prácticamente por la república islámica al inicio de la guerra.
Estados Unidos está aplicando en paralelo un bloqueo a los puertos iraníes, que dificulta la importación de gasolina.
El alto el fuego de abril puso fin a los combates más intensos, pero los ataques esporádicos, principalmente en el estrecho de Ormuz, ensombrecen las perspectivas de un acuerdo de paz duradero.
En un comunicado, el senador estadounidense Jack Reed criticó este viernes al presidente Donald Trump por la guerra.
"Seis meses después, no se ha alcanzado ni un solo objetivo", dijo Reed, el principal demócrata del Comité de Servicios Armados del Senado. "De hecho, ha debilitado significativamente nuestra posición en Oriente Medio y en el mundo", agregó.
Teherán mantiene desde hace semanas conversaciones con Omán sobre el futuro del estrecho de Ormuz, donde aspira a cobrar un peaje en concepto de "servicios" marítimos a los buques que transiten por él, algo

deduped_items.title: The US Wants to Get into Venezuelan Telecom (and Push China Out)
deduped_items.summary: Washington is allowing Venezuela to make telecommunications-related deals with American companies. But the Chinese must be left out
deduped_items.body_text:
The US Wants to Get into Venezuelan Telecom (and Push China Out)
Washington is allowing Venezuela to make telecommunications-related deals with American companies. But the Chinese must be left out
On August 21, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a couple of new general licences related to Venezuela’s telecommunications sector. Both General Licenses 61 and 62 will now allow the Venezuelan government (including but not limited to telecom authority CONATEL and State-owned telecom company CANTV) to acquire goods and services from and/or related to the US and authorize them to negotiate new contracts.
To better understand the implications of this on Venezuelan telecommunications, there’s what specialized local journalist William Peña wrote on Telecommunicaciones360. He concludes that “this opens an opportunity to the country in the issue of technologic updating, now it’s up to companies to have resources in order to accelerate their innovation process”.
The reaction from CONATEL to this announcement was so enthusiastic to the point of bragging that these licences “represent the recognition of the institutional legitimacy of the Venezuelan State” and that “these mechanisms reaffirm the intention of strengthening the infrastructure.”
Its press statement also mentioned the many areas that these couple of licenses will help to improve: from telephone and high-speed internet to subscription TV services and everything in relation to fiber optic cable networks, satellite transmission systems and submarine cable links.
The purchase of any non-US tech not explicitly banned is still subject to OFAC approval.
“Despite being the regulation authority, CONATEL is the one who disposes and provides the equipment for technical analysis of infrastructure and monitoring of the radioelectric spectrum,” Peña told Caracas Chronicles, later adding that “many of CONATEL’s current equipment is Chinese (in origin) and the Americans do not want that.”
Which leads to the main catch that the OFAC’s licences leave clear by explicitly forbidding: “Any transaction involving a person located in the Russian Federation, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, the Republic of Cuba, the People’s Republic of China, or any entity that is owned or controlled by or in a joint venture with such persons.”
The purchase of any non-US tech not explicitly banned is still subject to OFAC approval.
The same day the licenses were published, the State Department’s new Western Hemisphere chief, Juan Pablo Segura, tweeted that Chinese tech companies like Huawei, ZTE and several others “cooperate with Beijing’s intelligence services, creating risks of spying, hacking, and network shutdowns.” Ambassador Segura asked “US partners in the Americas to quickly switch to trusted suppliers to protect their people and their sovereignty.”
A deep relationship
This also comes with challenges for CANTV, which despite being the largest company in the sector, found itself behind in comparison to private companies because of several factors, including tUS sanctions that forced it to go with what other allies were offering.
Most of those countries mentioned were the only viable options that CANTV and other State entities were left with as a consequence of these sanctions. Peña notices their negative impact: “This process, with exceptions like some Chinese Huawei technologies, ended up harming the country’s progress in diverse areas, as beside the issue of language, many of the implemented solutions were not compatible with the technologies passed down and most were of very low quality regarding assets and software solutions. They carried many complications.”
The instruction from Washington to avoid China as a telecom provider was not missed by either the PRC’s embassy in DC or by Hong Kong’s major newspaper, the South China Morning Post, indicating that “the China carve-out could prove particularly consequential. Huawei and ZTE became impo

deduped_items.body_text:
Trump orders creation of US ‘Space Academy’, amid rivalry with China
The institution, which will train civilian and military recruits, will be modelled on the famous military school at West Point
US President Donald Trump on Friday announced the creation of a “Space Academy” to train future civilian and military recruits for an arena where the United States faces rivalry with China.
Speaking at Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, Trump said the institution would be modelled on the famed US military academy at West Point.
“It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal,” Trump said as he signed an executive order creating the new school.
“It’ll serve both the United States Space Force as well as Nasa and the civilian space flight industry, and it’ll attract, train, and graduate the very best of our nation.”
Trump has credited the US Space Force, the sixth branch of the US armed forces, with an important role in the recent American military operations in Venezuela and Iran.
He did not say where the new academy would be built.

deduped_items.body_text:
'All of a sudden the rug was pulled out': How Coyote vs. Acme went from the shelf to the big screen
In 2022, the cast and crew of Coyote vs. Acme attended a “funeral screening.”
It was as grim as it sounds. Warner Bros. had already announced the finished film was going to be forever shelved. Studio execs had controversially decided to take a $30-million tax writeoff as a cost-saving exercise rather than take on the expense of releasing and distributing it.
The film’s stars, Will Forte and Lana Condor, were among those went to the screening. The mood was not jubilant, to say the least, even though everyone was impressed with what they saw on the screen.
“That experience of watching the film was very layered,” says Condor, in a Zoom interview with Postmedia alongside Forte. “We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘”
“The shoot went great, we had been hearing the post-process was great, they were already testing it and the testing was going great,” adds Forte. “All of a sudden the rug was pulled out.”
“And so then when we watched the film and the credits rolled, there was this mass confusion and anger,” Condor says. “When credits rolled, we were like ‘This is a great movie! How is this possible?’”
After facing significant backlash and negative media coverage, the studio execs changed their minds and allowed an outside distributor to purchase the film. Enter Ketchup Entertainment, an independent film company that picked it up and held another screening before its wide release on Aug. 28.
The feeling was different the second time around.
“That was a great watch because we knew it was going to come out and it’s a great movie,” Condor says.
This strange chapter in the film’s behind-the-scenes story is being seen by some commentators as an indictment of the tone-deaf corporate indifference that seems to have overrun Hollywood studios these days. It is also strangely fitting for the tone of Coyote Vs. Acme, a story about corporate indifference and underdogs who never give up. Further vindication has come from early reviews, which have been largely positive. “Consistently funny and clever” proclaimed Brian Tallerico of rogerebert.com. “A cracking comedy that’s easily among the top ‘Looney Tunes’ movies ever,” writes Johnny Oleksinksi in the New York Post. “It’s smart, silly, and ultimately inspiring,” says Kristy Puchko of Mashable.com.
Directed by Dave Green and based on a satirical 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs. Acme blends animation and live-action in the spirit of Who Framed Roger Rabbit? Its central plot revolves around Wile E. Coyote’s decision to sue Acme, the massive corporation behind the endless trail of shoddy equipment he has used in his tireless pursuit of the Road Runner. He enlists the sad-eyed and defeated Kevin Avery (Forte) to represent him, an ambulance-chasing lawyer who specializes in getting small, out-of-court settlements from Acme for cartoon characters.
Avery is joined by his idealistic niece, Paige (played by Condor), who possesses unyielding enthusiasm and optimism for the case even though it pits them against a behemoth and heartless corporation fronted by a ruthless lawyer (played by former pro-wrestler Jon Cena).
“That experience of watching the film was very layered. We came in very confused and angry and thinking ‘well maybe, the film isn’t as great as we thought it was going to be … ‘
The mute Coyote shifts from the antagonist of the Looney Tunes shorts to a somewhat sympathetic character whose steadfast belief in his own genius despite years of failure becomes the endearing centre of the film. What follows is a story about friendship, loyalty and perseverance filled with slapstick humour, heart and appearances by a long line of Looney Tunes favourites. That includes everything from significant roles for Foghorn Leghorn and Tweety Bird to savvy bits featuring cameos by Pepe Le Pew, Gossamer and Dr. Lorre.

deduped_items.title: Tunisie: en pleine canicule, Kaïs Saïed dénonce des coupures d’eau et d’électricité «préméditées»
deduped_items.summary: En Tunisie, la canicule se poursuit cette semaine avec son lot de mécontentement social. Nouveaux délestages d’électricité face au pic de consommation dû à la chaleur, qui s’ajoutent à des coupures d’eau fréquentes ainsi qu’aux problèmes d’approvisionnement en eau en bouteille qui persistent. Même si la grogne sociale ne se traduit pas par des manifestations de grande ampleur, des mouvements spontanés de colère surviennent ponctuellement dans différentes régions de Tunisie et le ras-le-bol génér

Test yourself on the week of Aug. 22: A U.N. monitoring mission goes to Congo, the U.S. unveils an economic plan against Iran, and Putin issues a warning.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz!

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz!
1. In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what?
Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief.
2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee?
The peace deal brokered by Trump in eastern Congo to disarm M23 means nothing to locals—and many would prefer M23 remains, Krista Karch and Merveille Kavira Luneghe reported in January.
3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called?
If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue.
4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes?
Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues.
5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters?
The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month.
6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what?
The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.
7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime?
The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.
8. Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament on Thursday rejected the government’s proposed special military budget that would have focused on funding what?
Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo criticized the opposition’s plan as limiting Taipei’s ability to bolster its drone capabilities, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.
9. A humanoid robot set a new world record in the 100-meter dash at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Which human set the previous record of 9.58 seconds? (Hint: It was in 2009.)
The robot beat Bolt’s record by 0.19 seconds, slamming full speed into a padded wall and crashing to the ground to end its race, the New York Times reports.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz!
Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz!
1. In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what?
Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief.
2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee?
The peace deal brokered by Trump in eastern Congo to disarm M23 means nothing to locals—and many would prefer M23 remains, Krista Karch and Merveille Kavira Luneghe reported in January.
3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called?
If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue.
4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes?
Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues.
5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters?
The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month.
6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what?
The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.
7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime?
The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.
8. Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament on Thursday rejected the government’s proposed special military budget that would have focused on funding what?
Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo criticized the opposition’s plan as limiting Taipei’s ability to bolster its drone capabilities, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.
9. A humanoid robot set a new world record in the 100-meter dash at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Which human set the previous record of 9.58 seconds? (Hint: It was in 2009.)
The robot beat Bolt’s record by 0.19 seconds, slamming full speed into a padded wall and crashing to the ground to end its race, the New York Times reports.

2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee?
The peace deal brokered by Trump in eastern Congo to disarm M23 means nothing to locals—and many would prefer M23 remains, Krista Karch and Merveille Kavira Luneghe reported in January.
3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called?
If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue.
4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes?
Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues.
5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters?
The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month.
6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what?
The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.
7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime?
The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.
8. Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament on Thursday rejected the government’s proposed special military budget that would have focused on funding what?
Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo criticized the opposition’s plan as limiting Taipei’s ability to bolster its drone capabilities, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief.
9. A humanoid robot set a new world record in the 100-meter dash at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Which human set the previous record of 9.58 seconds? (Hint: It was in 2009.)
The robot beat Bolt’s record by 0.19 seconds, slamming full speed into a padded wall and crashing to the ground to end its race, the New York Times reports.

deduped_items.title: “The Strategy of Terrorism”
deduped_items.summary: A quarter century before 9/11, an upsurge in global terrorism prompted the historian David Fromkin to examine its purpose and method. Terrorism was a strategy of the weak, Fromkin wrote in these pages, but modern technology had enabled it “to enter the political arena on a new scale.” And its surprising success seemed to be due, in large part, “to a miscomprehension of the strategy by its opponents.”

deduped_items.body_text:
'No end in sight': Democrats slam Trump after six months of Iran war
US Democrats on Friday slammed the Trump administration for dragging out the war on Iran to its six month anniversary, warning Republicans would pay the price in the upcoming midterm elections.
The joint US-Israeli attack on Iran, beginning on 28 February, was initially meant to last a few weeks, by President Donald Trump's own estimates.
Half a year later, the war has seen the US lose at least 18 of its troops and cost $100bn in military spending, most of which was approved by the Republican-controlled Congress late last month after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth requested additional funds north of $60bn.
The war has cost each American taxpayer around $600 to $1,000 in extra energy costs because of Iran's response in blocking the Strait of Hormuz, according to a Brown University study and estimates from Moody's Analytics.
Estimates for the number of Iranian dead vary between 3,400, according to the UN’s OCHA agency, and 6,000, according to the Israeli military.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"Trump and his chief dealmaker [Vice President JD] Vance have failed to reach an agreement to end their war. Back in March, Trump and Vance said the war would be over 'soon' - but just this week, Trump said he is 'not in a hurry' to end the war," Democratic National Committee (DNC) chair Ken Martin said in a statement on Friday.
The DNC oversees all party activities and vets candidates for elections.
"[They] dragged the US into a deadly and costly war they clearly cannot find a way out of - at the expense of the American people who are struggling to make ends meet. Trump and Vance explicitly promised no new foreign wars, yet six months in, there is no end in sight to the conflict that has driven up prices on everything from gas to groceries," Martin said.
"While Republicans claim they cannot bring down costs or fund affordable healthcare for everyday Americans, they continue to spend billions of dollars on a war no one wanted or asked for - and voters will remember this betrayal when they head to the polls in November.”
The Silver Bulletin, which tracks and analyses public sentiment, noted on Friday that repeat polling has shown around 37 percent of Americans support the US-Israeli war on Iran, while 55 percent oppose it.
Half hearted opposition?
While Democrats in the House of Representatives latched onto an effort by the progressive wing of the party in late February to force a War Powers vote - which would insist on Congress having the power to declare war and not the president - it was not clear they would have actually opposed any attacks in their capacity as lawmakers.
Earlier this year, before the 28 February US-Israeli onslaught began, reports emerged that Democratic Party leadership was trying to curb more grassroots efforts to restrain Trump's war-making authority.
Establishment Democrats, many of whom failed to condemn Israel for what the United Nations and Holocaust scholars have called a genocide in Gaza, have not shied away from consistent condemnation of Iran, believing that, if not now, then at some point Tehran would have to be militarily confronted.
Iran itself had said that, while it must be ready for a war with the US - largely egged on by Israel - it would rather cut a deal that allows it the weapons it says it needs to defend itself as a sovereign state.
A week before the US and Israel began joint air strikes, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe briefed House and Senate leadership on the latest Iran developments behind closed doors.
The top Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, emerged only to say to reporters: "This is serious, and the administration has to make its case to the American people."

deduped_items.title: María Fernanda Espinosa: ‘We will not reform the UN by marginalising Africa’
deduped_items.summary: As the succession to António Guterres looms, Africa can no longer be reduced to its 54 votes. Its diversity, its political weight and its quest for autonomy must be fully taken into account by the next UN secretary-general, argues María Fernanda Espinosa, a candidate for the post.
deduped_items.body_text:
There is something in the way part of the world still talks about Africa at the United Nations that no longer fully matches the continent’s contemporary realities.
Here, its growing demographic weight is invoked; there, its promising economic growth. Then, all too often, attention fades away again, except when it comes to opportunistically courting its 54 votes in the major international forums.
Yet Africa cannot be viewed solely through the lens of its electoral weight or the crises it faces. Today, it is a space for diplomatic initiative, growth, and innovation, whose choices are increasingly helping to shape the international balance.
The succession to Guterres offers a historic opportunity to take better account of this shift.
In 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Liberia and Somalia sit on the Security Council. These countries will carry weight in a decision that will matter for the entire international system.
But their presence is above all a reminder of a deeper reality: whoever they are and wherever they come from, the next secretary-general will need to grasp Africa as it has become, not as it is sometimes still perceived through frameworks inherited from an international context that has now been left behind.
Changing the way we see Africa
Seeing Africa as it truly is calls for at least two shifts in perception. The first is that African unity is stronger than is often assumed.
On Security Council reform in particular, Africa has long made a clear demand: a continent of over a billion people cannot remain under-represented in some of the bodies where decisions with the heaviest consequences for its future and the world’s are taken.
This aspiration to fairer representation is, moreover, part of a broader debate on adapting multilateral institutions to the realities of the twenty-first century. But unity does not mean uniformity – the continent’s political diversity is very real.
This is partly where Africa’s political strength today comes from. Like many countries around the world, African states are seeking to preserve their decision-making capacity and diversify their partnerships in an increasingly complex international environment.
Dealing with Washington need not preclude a solid relationship with Beijing, Brussels, New Delhi, Ankara, Riyadh, Doha or other partners – and vice versa. This diversification is sometimes read as ambivalence, when in fact it often reflects a search for strategic autonomy and for partnerships suited to national and regional priorities.
Being able to engage with different partners, depending on the issue at hand and in keeping with one’s own priorities, has less to do with bloc logic than with a diplomatic pragmatism now visible in many regions of the world, from Africa to the Middle East, and across Asia and Latin America.
This is now a fundamental political factor for understanding Africa, and a reality the next secretary-general will need to reckon with if he or she is to help build a solid consensus for carrying through the organisation’s transformation.
In practical terms, this means it will be essential to sound out African positions before any strategic decision. It will also mean accepting that an African state may be supportive on one issue and far more distant on another.
As the fragmentation of the world order deepens, diplomacy will need to be capable of building convergence among states whose interests do not necessarily align on every front.
Rethinking the relationship with Africa
The second shift concerns the UN’s relationship with the continent itself. For decades, Africa has occupied a prominent place in the work of the United Nations, particularly in peacekeeping and peacebuilding, development and humanitarian action.
Yet many other issues that bear directly on the continent’s future would call for it to be more closely involved in strategic decisions – among them development financing, energy policy and the rules governing artificial intelligence.

deduped_items.title: بعد ستة أشهر من اندلاعها... ما أبرز تداعيات الحرب المتواصلة بين واشنطن وطهران؟
deduped_items.summary: أفرزت الحرب مع إيران تداعيات مكلفة لواشنطن وطهران. فبعد نحو ستة أشهر على الهجوم الذي شنته القوات الأمريكية والإسرائيلية على الجمهورية الإسلامية، وأسفر عن مقتل زعيمها الأعلى وإصابة نجله وخليفته بجروح خطيرة، تتعرض الحكومة الإيرانية لحصار اقتصادي، لكنها لا تزال ممسكة بزمام السلطة وتعتقد أن الوقت في صالحها. بالمقابل، يواجه الرئيس ترامب ضغوطا أكبر مع تراجع التأييد الشعبي للصراع قبل انتخابات التجديد النصفي في نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني، إذ يتعين على الحزب الجمهوري الدفاع عن أغلبية ضئيلة في مجلسي الكونغرس.

deduped_items.summary: أفرزت الحرب مع إيران تداعيات مكلفة لواشنطن وطهران. فبعد نحو ستة أشهر على الهجوم الذي شنته القوات الأمريكية والإسرائيلية على الجمهورية الإسلامية، وأسفر عن مقتل زعيمها الأعلى وإصابة نجله وخليفته بجروح خطيرة، تتعرض الحكومة الإيرانية لحصار اقتصادي، لكنها لا تزال ممسكة بزمام السلطة وتعتقد أن الوقت في صالحها. بالمقابل، يواجه الرئيس ترامب ضغوطا أكبر مع تراجع التأييد الشعبي للصراع قبل انتخابات التجديد النصفي في نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني، إذ يتعين على الحزب الجمهوري الدفاع عن أغلبية ضئيلة في مجلسي الكونغرس.

deduped_items.title: ¿Qué se sabe del secuestro de un militar de la Legión Extranjera francesa en Colombia?
deduped_items.summary: Según un informe del Ejército de Colombia, al que tuvo acceso la agencia de noticias AFP, se trata de un cabo identificado como José Olger Melo Charry, de doble nacionalidad: colombiana y francesa, perteneciente al cuerpo militar de élite de la nación europea. El hombre fue secuestrado a inicios de agosto, por un grupo de disidencias de las FARC, según la misma fuente, mientras se encontraba de visita en su país de origen. El caso pone en relieve el fortalecimiento de los grupos armados al marge

deduped_items.title: La isla de los leprosos: la historia de aislamiento de Nagashima, en Japón
deduped_items.summary: Este es un episodio de la historia de Japón poco conocido, incluso por los propios habitantes del archipiélago. En la década de 1930, el país emprendió una dura campaña contra la propagación de la lepra. Ante esta enfermedad infecciosa, que afecta principalmente los nervios y puede provocar lesiones y deformaciones, las autoridades japonesas optaron por aislar a los pacientes en sanatorios, entre ellos los de la isla de Nagashima. deduped_items.title: Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche: Beyond sorrow
deduped_items.summary: On the sidelines of the 2026 Rimini Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche, who have come to be known as “sisters in sorrow", speak to Vatican News about the tragedy that unites them. Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all

deduped_items.summary: On the sidelines of the 2026 Rimini Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche, who have come to be known as “sisters in sorrow", speak to Vatican News about the tragedy that unites them. Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all
